Matthew tells of Joseph's dream, of the child conceived "from the Holy Spirit",
and then steps back from the story to say what it means:

> "All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet:
> 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name
> Immanuel' (which means, God with us)." (Matthew 1:22–23)

The prophet is Isaiah, speaking to King Ahaz of Judah:

> "Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall
> conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." (Isaiah 7:14)

Micah 5:2, which Matthew reads of the Messiah's birthplace, is disputed too, but
there the dispute is only over whether the oracle looks forward at all (see the
argument "Born in Bethlehem"). Isaiah 7:14 is fought over more fiercely, and
the fight is about a word. Isaiah's Hebrew calls the woman an עַלְמָה (*almah*). Both sides grant
that the word names a young woman of marriageable age; they part over whether
it names a virgin. The Greek translation made by Jews before Christ, the
Septuagint, which Matthew quotes, renders it παρθένος, read as "virgin",
though whether the word meant that in the translator's own day is disputed
too. And the setting tells against Matthew's reading on its face. The sign is
given to Ahaz, and Isaiah 8:3–4 seems to fulfil it within the prophet's own
generation, so most critical scholarship, and much Jewish, reads 7:14 as having
nothing to do with a future Messiah.

So the question this argument asks is whether Scripture gives grounds for
holding that the Messiah would be born of a virgin, and which grounds survive
when every objection is heard (`messiahBornOfVirgin` is the claim it is about).

## Four strands, and a reply

The argument does not rest on Isaiah alone. It runs on four scriptural
strands, each from its own text, and each able to deliver the conclusion by
itself if its own disputed reading is granted.

- **Isaiah 7:14.** The prophecy Matthew quotes, read as foretelling a virgin
  birth. It turns on what *almah* means.
- **Genesis 3:15.** God tells the serpent that "her seed" will strike its head.
  The woman's seed, where Hebrew ordinarily reckons seed through the man, is
  read as marking a birth with no human father. Luther and Henry read it so.
  The Lutheran commentators Leupold and Keil, who hold the virgin birth, do
  not.
- **Micah 5:2–3.** The ruler from Bethlehem is born "when she who is in labour
  has given birth", a mother and no father named. The rival answer is
  immediate: that is an argument from silence, and an oracle about a woman in
  labour has no occasion to mention a father.
- **Isaiah 2–12.** Seth Postell reads 7:14 by its place in the finished book,
  between visions of the last days, as pointing to a future and miraculous
  birth.

Beside them stands a reply that delivers nothing of its own but takes away the
objection. *Almah* need not *mean* "virgin" for Mary to *be* an *almah*.
Rebekah is called an עַלְמָה at Genesis 24:43 and a virgin "whom no man had
known" at 24:16, the same woman under both words. Mary was a betrothed young
woman who conceived as a virgin, so she answers Isaiah's description on anyone's
dictionary. The chapter [Four strands, and what each depends on](born-of-a-virgin/the-strands.md) takes the
strands and this reply in turn.

What the checking found, taken together, is this. Remove the reading of
*almah* and the other three strands still reach the conclusion
(`almah_not_load_bearing`). Remove the disputed reading from all four and it
fails (`hinges_jointly_load_bearing`). So no single disputed word decides the
argument. That does not make any strand's reading secure: each is contested,
and the later chapters say by whom.

A fifth route is encoded and kept apart. Papal teaching on Mary's virginity, as
Mark Miravalle collates it, settles the question for a Roman Catholic, and the
`catholic` package holds it. This library's author does not grant that
magisterial teaching settles doctrinal questions, and the encoding says so
rather than folding it in. For a reader who does not grant it, that route
yields nothing on its own (`magisterial_authority_is_load_bearing`), and the
rival is cited to the Westminster Confession, I.x.

## The questions the later chapters take

- **Was Isaiah's sign only for Ahaz?** The critic's case is that a sign for
  Ahaz's own day cannot also foretell a virgin birth. Heard alone against the
  scriptural reading, nothing prevails. Heard with the replies of Berry,
  Postell and Motyer, the scriptural reading prevails, and the verdict rests on
  Postell's two counterexamples ([Was Isaiah's sign only for Ahaz?](born-of-a-virgin/ahaz.md)).
- **Does Isaiah's grammar say the woman was already pregnant?** Paul Wegner
  argues so, and that a pregnant woman is no virgin. His argument is valid, and
  it needs the pregnancy to be an ordinary one. Supplied from his own reading of
  the sign, it goes round in a circle. The fathers answer that an ordinary
  conception is no sign at all, and that dispute ties
  ([Was the woman already pregnant?](born-of-a-virgin/wegner.md)).
- **Doesn't the Septuagint's "virgin" settle it?** Its witness prevails over
  Wegner's account of the Greek word, but it shows how one early reader read
  Isaiah, not what Isaiah's word means, and it leaves the conception itself
  open ([What the Septuagint's word meant](born-of-a-virgin/septuagint.md)).
- **What does Scripture itself make of the word?** Matthew quotes the Greek of a
  woman who conceived before she and Joseph came together. Under the standard
  that Scripture interprets Scripture his reading prevails; under the evidence
  standard it ties with Wegner ([Matthew's reading of the word](born-of-a-virgin/matthew.md)).
- **Does "her seed" mean no human father?** Luther says the wording means it;
  Leupold and Lewis deny it, and that dispute ties
  ([Does Genesis 3:15 rule out a human father?](born-of-a-virgin/her-seed.md)).
- **Is Genesis 3:15 a promise, fulfilled in Jesus?** Every term of the verse is
  met as the New Testament names it. Against Westermann, who denies that the
  verse is any promise, nothing prevails as the evidence weighs it, and the
  fulfilment prevails under the Scripture standard
  ([Is Genesis 3:15 a promise, fulfilled in Jesus?](born-of-a-virgin/the-promise.md)).

The claims themselves, each with its number, its source and its rating, are
listed in the appendix, "The claims and their sources".

#### Where things are

that no one could hold in view. The dependencies run one way. Where a file
outgrew three hundred lines of code, the material for the disputes over Wegner's
objection, over the Septuagint's word and over the woman's seed, and the
citations for the dispute over the critical denial, went into modules of their
own beside it.
